opus-5.5.text:
Look, I think the simplest way to think about it is to just count the orders of magnitude. If you go from GPT-2 to GPT-4, that's roughly preschooler to smart high schooler in about four years. And when you decompose where that came from, you've got three big drivers. First, raw compute: we've been scaling training compute at something like half an order of magnitude per year, way faster than Moore's law, because people are just spending enormously more on clusters. Second, algorithmic efficiency: better architectures, better training recipes, and data tricks that give you another roughly half an order of magnitude a year in effective compute. And third, what I call "unhobbling." The base models are incredibly smart in some ways but hobbled in really dumb ways. Things like RLHF, chain-of-thought, tools, and longer context unlock latent capability that was already there.

So if you just trace those lines forward, you get another GPT-2-to-GPT-4-sized jump by around 2027. Maybe more than that, actually, once you account for the unhobbling. And I think that gets you to models that can do the work of an AI researcher or engineer. Not a chatbot you ask questions, but something more like a drop-in remote worker. You onboard it, it has context on your codebase, it works on a problem for weeks, and it comes back with results.

That's the critical threshold, because once you can automate AI research itself, you might have hundreds of millions of these automated researchers running at many times human speed. Then you could compress a decade of algorithmic progress into a year or less. That's the intelligence explosion. You go from roughly human-level to vastly superhuman pretty quickly.

Now, there's real uncertainty. The data wall is a real question. We're running out of internet text, and whether synthetic data, self-play, and RL approaches work at scale is the big open research bet. But the labs are pouring everything into it, and historically betting against deep learning has been a losing trade. So my rough view is that AGI by 2027 is strikingly plausible. It's not certain, but it's plausible enough that we should be taking it very seriously. That means thinking about the trillion-dollar clusters, the power buildout, security at the labs, and what this means for national security. Very few people are really pricing that in yet.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the cleanest way to see it is to just count the orders of magnitude. GPT-2 to GPT-4 took us from a model that could barely string together coherent sentences, basically a preschooler, to something that's a smart high schooler, that can write code, that can pass the bar exam. That happened in about four years. And when you decompose what drove it, it's mostly three things: raw compute scaleup, algorithmic efficiencies, and then what I'd call unhobbling, which is going from a base model that's basically autocomplete to chatbots, to RLHF, to chain of thought, to tools. Each of those is worth multiple orders of magnitude of effective compute.

So the question is just, do those trends continue? And I think the answer is pretty clearly yes for the next few years. Compute is the easiest one to see. The clusters are being built right now. You can read the earnings calls. We're going from tens of thousands of GPUs to hundreds of thousands to millions, and the training runs are going from ten-megawatt to gigawatt scale. Algorithmic progress has been running at something like half an order of magnitude a year, pretty consistently, and there's no reason to think the labs are out of ideas. And on unhobbling, I think the big thing people underrate is that the models today are still fundamentally chatbots. You give them a prompt, they give you an answer, they forget everything. The next step is agents, models that can work on a problem for hours or days, that can use a computer, that have onboarding and context the way a new employee does. That's not a new paradigm, it's just removing obvious limitations.

If you add it all up, you get another GPT-2 to GPT-4 sized jump by roughly 2027. And a GPT-4 sized jump on top of a smart high schooler lands you at something like a PhD or an expert, and more importantly, something that can do the job of an AI researcher or engineer. That's the thing I'd really draw attention to, because that's where it stops being a smooth curve. Once you can run millions of copies of automated researchers, each one thinking much faster than a human, you compress what would have been a decade of algorithmic progress into a year or so. And that's how you get from AGI to something quite a bit beyond us very quickly.

Now, I want to be honest that the error bars here are big. It's possible we hit a data wall, it's possible the unhobbling runs out and the models stay stuck as this weird sort of brilliant-but-useless thing. But I think the base case, just trend-extrapolating, is that by 2027 the models are doing serious cognitive work, and the people in San Francisco building them think that too. The surprising thing to me is less that it might happen and more how few people outside those buildings are taking it seriously.

astra-6.text:
I think the next few years could be pretty extraordinary. The way I’d approach this is to look at the trend: models have gone from barely being able to put together coherent paragraphs to writing code and solving fairly difficult problems. Then ask what happens as we put more compute into training, improve the algorithms, and give these systems more time to reason through a task.

My expectation is that we’ll move from systems that answer questions to systems that can actually carry out substantial projects. There’s still a big gap there. Being able to solve a coding problem doesn’t mean you can work reliably as a software engineer for a week. But closing that gap doesn’t necessarily require some entirely new scientific breakthrough.

So I take AGI within the next few years seriously, though I wouldn’t pretend we can pin down a date. The particularly consequential threshold is when these systems can help automate AI research itself. At that point, you have a feedback loop: better AI helps you build better AI. That could make the pace of progress much faster than people are expecting.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the way to approach this is to take the trend seriously. We’ve gone from models that could barely put together a coherent paragraph to models that can write code, reason through difficult problems, and do useful work. The question is what happens if we get several more years of progress at anything like that pace.

There are a few things driving it: more compute, better algorithms, and figuring out how to get more useful work out of the capabilities models already have. A model might be quite smart in a short interaction but still struggle to carry out a project over several days. Improving reliability, memory, and the ability to use tools could make a big difference even without a dramatic jump in underlying intelligence.

So I take seriously the possibility that, within the next few years, we’ll have systems that can do much of the intellectual work a human can do. That’s uncertain, particularly when it comes to long, messy tasks. But the really consequential threshold is when these systems can help automate AI research itself. Then you’re no longer just extrapolating the previous pace of progress—the process producing that progress starts to change.
